claims.text: The proposed intervention is annealing HfZrTiTa0.53 at approximately 600 °C for about 4 hours.
Controlled cooling after annealing will avoid premature precipitate coarsening.
Annealing HfZrTiTa0.53 at 600 °C for 4 hours will cause ultrafine precipitates to nucleate and grow along grain boundaries.
The annealing-induced grain-boundary precipitates will be ductile.
The ultrafine precipitates will relieve local tensile stress concentrations.
The ultrafine precipitates will act as dislocation-nucleation centers during tensile deformation.
The precipitates will delay crack initiation and propagation.
Grain-boundary precipitation will promote more homogeneous plastic flow.
The annealing treatment will improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation in HfZrTiTa0.53.
Uniform tensile elongation may increase by more than 10% relative to the untreated baseline.
The annealing treatment will preserve approximately the untreated alloy's yield strength.
The annealing treatment will preserve impact-triggered energy release.
As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a yield strength of 786 MPa.
As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has a compressive strength of 1314 MPa.
As-processed HfZrTiTa0.53 has approximately 13.5% terminal strain.
The reported 13.5% terminal strain represents limited tensile ductility.
The proposed effect applies at room temperature under quasi-static tension near a strain rate of 1×10^-4 s^-1.
The beneficial treatment window is approximately 500–700 °C for several hours.
Treatments outside the proposed temperature-time window may degrade strength or impact properties through coarsening or related microstructural changes.
Charpy impact energy can establish preservation of the alloy's impact-triggered energetic response.

contradictions.description: The 13.5% value is called terminal strain in the baseline but is treated as evidence of limited tensile ductility and as the reference for uniform tensile elongation. Terminal strain, tensile terminal elongation, and uniform elongation are not established as the same measurement.

The hypothesis requires preservation of impact-triggered chemical energy release, but the proposed impact measurement is Charpy absorbed energy, which measures mechanical impact toughness rather than chemical energy release during penetration.
